senses.definition: The person who argues your case in rooms you are not in.
senses.caution: Naming someone as yours assigns them work they may not have agreed to, and in a hierarchy it can expose them - a director who is quietly helpful may not want to be described that way in front of their peers. Said of yourself about a cause it is fine; said of yourself about your own interests it sounds like a job title you invented. With lawyers in the room the word means counsel and will be heard that way first.
senses.example: We don't need everyone convinced. We need one advocate on that committee who'll say it when we're not in the room.

cues.text: You are told the committee will decide without you present, and you want the word for the one person in there who will make your case.
A mentor asks what you actually need from her, and the honest answer is someone who will speak for the work when you are not there to speak for it.
Your grandmother's hospital appointments go badly when she attends alone, and you want the word for the role a family member plays by going with her.
You are describing a teacher who fought the school on your son's behalf for two years, and you want the word for what she was to him.

distractors: The most senior people in an organisation, spoken of as one group.
A voluntary group of people who do the same work and swap what they know.
A rule of thumb that usually works well enough.
An isolated environment where code runs safely.
The one you actually use every day.

senses.definition: To argue openly for a position or a person, putting your own standing behind it.
senses.caution: It spends credibility, and it spends it visibly. Claiming it ties you to the outcome, so keep it for the two or three things a year you would still defend after they went wrong. Used about a small preference it inflates the stakes, and in a written self-assessment it reads as claiming credit unless the thing worked. There is also a floor: if all you did was agree in a meeting, someone who was there will remember that.
senses.example: I advocated for keeping the evaluation in-house, and knowing what it cost us, I'd make the same call again.

cues.text: In a performance conversation you need a verb for the handful of times you put your own name behind an unpopular position rather than simply agreeing with it.
A junior colleague's work was passed over and you intend to raise it with the panel yourself, at some cost to your own standing.
You are pressing the council to fix a dangerous junction by the school, and it has turned into a campaign rather than a complaint.
A relative needs a treatment the insurer keeps refusing, and somebody in the family has to make the case, loudly and repeatedly.

distractors: To speak about someone in a way that lowers them, usually with a passing remark.
To make a bad situation worse.
To avoid something on purpose when you could have taken it.
To make something already written finally make sense by laying out the reasoning.
To turn a structure that only exists in memory into a form you can store or send on.
